chapter.title: A share is a slice of a shop

cards.body: Buy one share of a company and you legally own part of it. How much? Picture the market as **one big organised bazaar**: every company is a shop, a share is one tiny slice of one shop, and the price on the board is simply what the last buyer and seller shook hands on.
cards.simpler: When you buy one share of a company, you own a small piece of it. Think of the whole stock market as **one big organised bazaar**. Each company is a shop in that bazaar. A share is one tiny slice of one shop. The price you see on the board is just the number the last buyer and seller agreed on when they made their deal.

cards.prompt: Asha buys 1 share of a biscuit company that is cut into 100 crore equal slices. What does Asha own now?

options.text: A right to free biscuits, like a loyalty card
One hundred-crore-th of the whole company, profits and all
A loan the company must pay back with interest

whyNot.a: That's a customer perk, not ownership: owning a slice gives you a share of profits, not products.
whyNot.c: That's a bond, not a share: a lender gets interest and their money back, an owner gets a slice of whatever the shop earns.

cards.reteach: A share is literally a share: the company is cut into equal pieces and you hold one. If the shop makes a profit, a sliver of it belongs to you. Nobody owes you the money back, because you are not a lender. You are a part-owner.

cards.title: What you actually hold
cards.body:
A listed company cuts itself into millions, often billions, of equal slices and sells some to the public. **One share is one of those slices.** It sits in your name, and you can sell it to anyone who wants it.

Ownership brings two things. If the company hands out profit, called a *dividend*, you get your sliver. At the yearly meeting you get a vote, one per share. With 1 share your vote is a whisper in a stadium. It still counts.

The company gets your money only once, when it first sells the slice. After that you trade with other owners, not with the shop.
cards.simpler: A company on the stock market cuts itself into millions of equal slices and sells some to the public. **One share is one of those slices.** You can sell it to anyone. If the company pays out profit, called a dividend, you get your part. You also get one vote per share at the yearly meeting. The company gets your money only once, at the first sale. After that you trade with other owners, not the company.

cards.title: Tuesday in Pune, Wednesday in Kochi
cards.body: Ravi, a dentist in Pune, buys 1 share of a paint company at ₹2,400 on Tuesday. The company does not notice. It does not get his ₹2,400 either; a stranger in Kochi who was selling does. Wednesday, the share is at ₹2,352, down 2%. **Nothing changed inside the company.** Fewer people wanted paint-company slices that morning than wanted to get rid of them, and the sellers kept dropping their asking price until someone bit.
cards.simpler: Ravi is a dentist in Pune. On Tuesday he buys one share of a paint company for ₹2,400. The company does not notice, and it does not get his money. A stranger in Kochi who was selling gets it. On Wednesday the share is at ₹2,352, down 2%. **Nothing changed inside the company.** That morning, fewer people wanted to buy paint-company slices than wanted to sell them. So the sellers kept lowering their price until someone said yes.

cards.prompt: At 11 am a cement company announces it won a giant highway contract. Within minutes 10 people want to buy its shares for every 1 who wants to sell. What happens, and why?

options.text: The price rises, because good news automatically adds value to the shares
The price rises, because buyers must offer more to tempt the few sellers
Nothing yet, because the company has to publish its new price first

whyNot.a: That's the headline, not the mechanism: news only moves a price by changing how many people want to buy versus sell.
whyNot.c: That's a shop with a price tag, not the bazaar: the company never sets its own share price, buyers and sellers do.

cards.reteach: Think of 10 people shouting for 1 slice. The holder won't sell at the old price when there's a queue. Someone offers more, then someone offers more than that. The price on the board is just the latest deal, so it climbs. Flip the numbers and it falls.

cards.title: Why the number never sits still
cards.body:
You'd think the price shows what a company is worth. It doesn't. **It shows the last price at which one buyer and one seller agreed.** That is all. The board updates every time a new pair agrees, which on a busy share is many times a second.

So the only question that explains a move is: who was keener today, buyers or sellers? More buyers than sellers, and buyers bid higher to get in. More sellers than buyers, and sellers accept less to get out. Headlines, results, rumours, rain: they matter only through that one door.

Note the shopkeeper's silence. The company cannot raise or cut its share price. It can only do things that change who wants in.
cards.simpler: You might think the share price shows what a company is worth. It does not. **It shows the last price one buyer and one seller agreed on.** The number changes every time a new pair agrees. So ask one question: who wanted it more today, buyers or sellers? More buyers, and they offer more to get in. More sellers, and they accept less to get out. News matters only through that door. The company cannot set its own price.

cards.body: Priya reads that a bank posted record profit, buys at 9:20, and watches it drop 4% by lunch. She assumes the news was fake. It wasn't. Big holders had expected even bigger profit and used the morning rush of buyers to sell into it. Spot the trap: whenever you say 'it should go up', ask instead **who is selling, and why would they stop?**
cards.simpler: Priya reads that a bank made record profit. She buys at 9:20 and watches the price fall 4% by lunch. She thinks the news must have been false. It was true. People who owned lots of shares had hoped for even bigger profit. They used the morning rush of buyers as a chance to sell. Here is the trap. Whenever you catch yourself saying 'it should go up', ask instead **who is selling, and why would they stop?**

cards.prompt: A share closed 3% lower today. Which one-line explanation uses this chapter's idea?

options.text: The company cut its share price by 3% to attract buyers
More people wanted to sell than buy, so sellers kept accepting a little less until the day ended
The company lost 3% of its factories, so each slice shrank

whyNot.a: That's the shopkeeper setting a tag, which never happens: the company has no price button, only buyers and sellers do.
whyNot.c: That's confusing the slice with the shop: your share is still the same fraction of the company, only the price people pay for it changed.

cards.reteach: Your slice never shrinks or grows; you own the same fraction tomorrow as today. What changes is what the next person will pay for it. A fall simply means today's sellers outnumbered buyers and had to accept less to find one.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A share is one equal slice of a company, and it stays the same size whatever the price does. The price is just **the last deal** between a buyer and a seller, so it rises when buyers outnumber sellers and falls when sellers outnumber buyers.

Tomorrow: India has two bazaars selling identical slices. Guess how far their prices differ.
cards.simpler: A share is one equal slice of a company. The slice stays the same size no matter what the price does. The price is only **the last deal** between a buyer and a seller. So it goes up when more people want to buy than sell. It goes down when more people want to sell than buy. Tomorrow: India has two bazaars selling the very same slices. Guess how far apart their prices are.

cards.body: Tomorrow between 9:15 am and 3:30 pm, search 'Reliance share price' on your phone. Watch the number for 60 seconds and count the changes. Each change is **one buyer and one seller** agreeing on a new number. Nothing else.
cards.simpler: Tomorrow, some time between 9:15 in the morning and 3:30 in the afternoon, search 'Reliance share price' on your phone. Watch the number for one minute and count how many times it changes. Every change means **one buyer and one seller** just agreed on a new number. That is the whole story. Nothing else is moving it.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain in one line why a share rose or fell today, using buyers and sellers rather than headlines.
